name: Bangkok
tagline: Gilded temples, river palaces and endless street feasts.
whenBlurb: Come November to February, when the air turns cool and dry; skip April's fierce heat and the June-to-October monsoon downpours.

ourTake.lede: Bangkok rewards the traveller who slows down and moves by boat and on foot rather than fighting the traffic all day. Do the Grand Palace and Wat Pho early, then let the river and the side-streets carry the rest; the food, from street stalls to Michelin rooms, is the real headline. November to February is the window when the heat eases enough to enjoy being out.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a great-value luxury city break - fine hotels, brilliant food and easy visa-free entry.
ourTake.skipIf: You want quiet and calm; Bangkok is loud, dense and always in motion.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Capella Bangkok
items.description: The house the world voted its very best, a low, garden-wrapped sanctuary on the river's quiet bend.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Bangkok at Chao Phraya River
items.description: Tiered lawns stepping down to the water, and the surest service in the city.

items.name: Aman Nai Lert Bangkok
items.description: Aman's return to Thailand, a hushed tower rising from century-old parkland in the heart of town.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Bangkok
items.description: The city's grande dame since 1876, the address every other Bangkok hotel is measured against.

items.name: The Siam
items.description: An Art Deco riverside retreat of just 39 suites and pool villas, a private-collector's house, not a hotel.

items.name: The Peninsula Bangkok
items.description: A W-shaped tower built to give every room the river, and a fleet of green Peninsula boats at the jetty.

items.name: Rosewood Bangkok
items.description: Two hands clasped in the wai, rendered as a tower, vertical, arty and quietly grand.

items.name: The Sukhothai Bangkok
items.description: Lotus ponds, teak and brick pavilions, a low-rise pocket of old Siam in the business district.

items.name: The Okura Prestige Bangkok
items.description: Japanese precision poured into a Bangkok tower, with a cantilevered 25th-floor pool over the city.

items.name: Park Hyatt Bangkok
items.description: A tailored city house set atop the Central Embassy mall, refined, discreet, effortlessly connected.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Bangkok
items.description: The Ritz-Carlton's Bangkok debut inside the pixelated MahaNakhon tower, high, sleek and central.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Bangkok
items.description: Art Deco New York glamour in a lotus-inspired tower, above the Ratchaprasong shopping heart.

items.name: The St. Regis Bangkok
items.description: Butler service and racecourse views on Ratchadamri, connected straight to the BTS.

items.name: Anantara Siam Bangkok Hotel
items.description: Hand-painted murals, a lush pool courtyard and old-Bangkok grace off the busiest corner in town.

items.name: Dusit Thani Bangkok
items.description: The reborn golden-spire landmark, a homegrown grande dame, rebuilt for a new century.

items.name: Kimpton Maa-Lai Bangkok
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice, No. 2 Hotel in Bangkok (2023)
items.description: A playful, design-forward tower on a leafy lane beside Lumphini Park.

items.name: COMO Metropolitan Bangkok
items.description: Understated urban minimalism and the wellness rigour COMO is known for.

items.name: InterContinental Bangkok
items.description: A dependable, well-run city tower plugged directly into Bangkok's shopping arteries.

items.name: 137 Pillars Suites & Residences Bangkok
items.description: An all-suite colonial-teak homage, with a vertigo-edge rooftop pool over Sukhumvit.

items.name: Oriental Residence Bangkok
items.description: A discreet all-suite address with kitchens, an apartment's ease with a hotel's polish.

items.name: SO/ Bangkok
items.description: A colour-splashed design tower overlooking the green of Lumphini Park.

items.name: The Grand Palace & Wat Phra Kaew (Temple of the Emerald Buddha)
items.description: Bangkok's single most important sight: the walled royal city of the Chakri kings, its glittering spires and murals surrounding the tiny, revered Emerald Buddha. Go at opening (8:30am) to beat the heat and coach crowds; a licensed private guide turns a crowded shuffle into a genuinely legible morning, and there is a strict cover-shoulders-and-knees dress code for the whole family.

items.name: Wat Pho (Temple of the Reclining Buddha)
items.description: A short walk south of the Grand Palace, home to the 46-metre gold-leaf Reclining Buddha and the birthplace of traditional Thai massage. End the visit with a proper hour-long massage at the on-site school for a fraction of a spa price. Open daily to 6:30pm, calmer in late afternoon.

items.name: Wat Arun (Temple of Dawn)
items.description: The porcelain-encrusted Khmer-style prang rising from the west bank, best reached by the two-minute cross-river ferry from Tha Tien pier. Climb the steep steps for river views, then time your visit for golden hour when the spire glows; the reverse view from a Tha Tien rooftop bar at sunset is the classic photograph.

items.name: Wat Saket & the Golden Mount
items.description: A gentle spiral of about 320 steps winds up Bangkok's only hill, past bells and prayer flags to a gold chedi and a 360-degree panorama over the Old Town rooftops. One of the finest free sunset perches in the city and refreshingly uncrowded.

items.name: Wat Traimit (Temple of the Golden Buddha)
items.description: Houses a 5.5-tonne solid-gold Buddha, over three metres tall, hidden under plaster for centuries and revealed by accident. Sits at the gateway to Chinatown, so pair it with a Yaowarat food crawl. The upstairs galleries tell the story of the Chinese community in Bangkok.

items.name: Wat Benchamabophit (The Marble Temple)
items.description: Built of white Carrara marble imported from Italy, this is the temple on the back of the old five-baht coin and one of Bangkok's most photogenic yet least crowded. The cloister of 52 Buddha images in different regional styles is a quiet, serene stop away from the tourist trail.

items.name: Wat Ratchanatdaram & Loha Prasat (The Metal Castle)
items.description: A 37-spired iron 'metal castle', the only structure of its kind still standing, its tapering black spires unlike anything else in Bangkok. Climb the spiral staircase past meditation cloisters to a top-level walkway with views to the Golden Mount and Democracy Monument.

items.name: Jim Thompson House
items.description: The teak compound of the American 'Silk King' who revived the Thai silk trade then vanished in 1967, assembled from six antique houses and filled with Southeast Asian art. A garden oasis minutes from the shopping malls, with excellent guided tours, a serene café and a shop of genuinely good silk for gifts.

items.name: Museum of Contemporary Art (MOCA Bangkok)
items.description: A private five-floor, 20,000-square-metre museum holding one of Thailand's finest collections of modern and contemporary Thai art, anchored by the works Thawan Duchanee. Air-conditioned, spacious and unhurried, it is an easy afternoon and a genuine highlight for art-minded travellers.

items.name: Bangkok National Museum
items.description: Southeast Asia's largest museum, set in a former palace, spanning Thai history from prehistory through the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms, including the royal funeral chariots. Free English-language volunteer guided tours a few mornings a week are the best way to make sense of it before the temples.

items.name: Suan Pakkad Palace
items.description: A cluster of eight antique teak houses assembled by a prince and princess into a serene garden museum, its jewel the lacquer-and-gold Ban Chiang Lacquer Pavilion. Rarely busy, it is a graceful, discreet stop for those who found Jim Thompson's crowds too much.

items.name: Rattanakosin (Old Town) walk
items.description: The historic royal island threaded by canals, where the palaces, temples and old shophouses of Bangkok's founding cluster within walking distance. Wander from the Grand Palace past amulet markets, the giant swing at Wat Suthat and Sao Ching Cha, ideally early morning before the heat, on foot or by tuk-tuk.

items.name: Yaowarat (Chinatown) after dark
items.description: Bangkok's most electric street-food strip: after sunset the neon comes on and woks roar along Yaowarat Road and its side lanes. Come hungry for seafood, dim sum, bird's-nest and mango sticky rice, and duck into the gold shops and old Chinese shrines. A guided evening food walk cuts through the chaos and can be tailored for vegetarian and Jain diners.

items.name: Talat Noi
items.description: One of Bangkok's oldest quarters, a maze of Chinese shophouses, car-part workshops, hidden shrines, street art and hip cafés that rewards slow wandering by foot or bicycle. The riverside lanes here are genuinely atmospheric and refreshingly untouristed compared with Yaowarat.

items.name: Charoen Krung & Bang Rak creative district
items.description: Bangkok's first paved street, now the city's creative heart, where legendary street stalls sit beside boundary-pushing restaurants, galleries and the Warehouse 30 and TCDC design hubs. A good half-day of gallery-hopping, riverside cafés and boutique shopping for design-minded travellers.

items.name: Thonglor & Ekkamai
items.description: Where affluent young Bangkok goes out: sleek wine bars, speakeasies, live-music rooms, top Japanese restaurants and upscale community malls like The Commons. The most polished, discreet nightlife in the city and a natural base for travellers staying in the modern Sukhumvit hotels.

items.name: Ari
items.description: A leafy, low-rise neighbourhood of independent cafés, small design shops and easygoing restaurants that feels like a village inside the megacity. Best explored on a slow morning of coffee-hopping, and blessedly quiet compared with Sukhumvit.

items.name: Chatuchak Weekend Market
items.description: One of the world's largest markets: some 15,000 stalls across 35 acres of clothing, antiques, art, ceramics, plants and a serious food scene. Go early on a Saturday or Sunday to beat the heat, note the numbered sections so you can find your way back, and treat it as the city's great treasure hunt.

items.name: Chao Phraya river & the express boat
items.description: The river is Bangkok's original highway and the best way to link the big riverside sights. Hop the tourist or local express boat between Sathorn, the Old Town temples and ICONSIAM for a breezy, cheap, ever-changing view of barges, temples and skyscrapers. A private long-tail charter gives a family the same views on its own schedule.

items.name: Thonburi canal (khlong) long-tail boat tour
items.description: Slip off the main river into the quiet canals of Thonburi, past stilt houses, orchid gardens, riverside temples and the giant Buddha of Wat Paknam. The classic 'Venice of the East' experience; a private long-tail lets you set the pace and stop at the Artist's House (Baan Silapin) for coffee and a puppet show.

items.name: Chao Phraya dinner cruise
items.description: A two-hour glide past the floodlit Grand Palace, Wat Arun and the bridges, with Thai and international dinner service on board. The premium cruises are a genuinely lovely, low-effort evening for multi-generational groups; book a window or open-deck table and confirm vegetarian menus in advance.

items.name: Mahanakhon SkyWalk & Sky Bar
items.description: Bangkok's highest public viewpoint on the 78th floor of King Power Mahanakhon (about 314 metres), including a glass-floor tray for the brave and an open rooftop bar. The clearest, most modern panorama of the whole city, best at dusk as the lights come on.

items.name: Sky Bar at Lebua (State Tower)
items.description: The golden-domed rooftop bar made famous by 'The Hangover Part II', perched 63 floors above the Chao Phraya with an unmatched sweep of the river bend. A smart-casual dress code applies and cocktails are premium-priced; come for the view and the occasion rather than the value.

items.name: Vertigo & Moon Bar (Banyan Tree)
items.description: An open-air rooftop restaurant and bar on the 61st floor with a 360-degree horizon and no glass to spoil the view. The most romantic of the sky bars for a couple; book a railing table a few days ahead for sunset.

items.name: Lumpini Park
items.description: Bangkok's first and best-loved park, a green lung of lakes, jogging paths, banyan trees and resident monitor lizards in the heart of the business district. Come at dawn for the tai chi and free open-air aerobics, or rent a pedal boat with the children in the late afternoon.

items.name: Benjakitti Forest Park
items.description: A striking rewilded wetland park with elevated walkways over lotus ponds and reed beds, so lush that rare birds have returned to the city. Linked to Lumpini by the elevated 'Green Mile' skywalk, it is a superb early-morning walk or run right next to the Sukhumvit hotels.

items.name: Bang Krachao (Bangkok's Green Lung)
items.description: An artificial-island loop of jungle, mangrove and canal just across the river, laced with raised concrete cycle paths through backyard gardens. Rent a bicycle, visit the floating Bang Nam Phueng weekend market and Sri Nakhon Khuean Khan Park; the closest thing to countryside within reach of downtown.

items.name: Wat Paknam Phasi Charoen
items.description: A 69-metre seated Buddha towers over the canals, but the real wonder is the fifth-floor emerald glass stupa beneath a cosmic ceiling mural that has made this one of Bangkok's most photographed temples. Still set in a genuinely local canal-side neighbourhood, it pairs naturally with a Thonburi boat tour.

items.name: Erawan Museum
items.description: A colossal three-headed bronze elephant crowns a museum whose interior is an extravagant journey from an underworld basement up through an earthly floor to a heaven of stained glass and a spiral staircase. The eccentric vision of collector Lek Viriyaphant; a memorable, unusual stop for families en route to the Ancient City.

items.name: Ancient City (Muang Boran)
items.description: An enormous open-air park shaped like Thailand, dotted with over 100 scaled replicas and restorations of the country's greatest monuments. Rent a golf cart or bicycle and cover the whole kingdom in an afternoon; a clever, uncrowded outing with older children who found the city temples tiring.

items.name: ICONSIAM
items.description: A vast riverside luxury mall with global flagships, a landmark waterfront and the indoor SookSiam floating-market food hall recreating all 77 provinces under one roof. The nightly musical fountain show on the river is free; a good rainy-afternoon or air-conditioned family stop with genuinely broad dining, including easy vegetarian options.

items.name: Asiatique The Riverfront
items.description: A converted riverside warehouse district of shops, restaurants and a big Ferris wheel, reached by a free shuttle boat from Sathorn pier as the sun sets over the water. An easy, relaxed evening for families, with the option of a ladyboy cabaret or Muay Thai Live show on site.

items.name: Jodd Fairs night market
items.description: Bangkok's buzziest night market of the moment, over 1,500 white-tent stalls of street food, drinks and clothing beside the MRT, famous for the leaning-tower 'volcano' pork ribs. Come hungry after 6pm; lively, young and easy to reach by metro.

items.name: Talad Rot Fai (Train Night Market), Srinakarin
items.description: A sprawling vintage-and-antiques night market of retro cars, warehouse bars, collectibles and food, best seen from the overlooking rooftop bars where the rows of tents glow at night. More characterful and less polished than the mall night markets, open Thursday to Sunday evenings.

items.name: Rajadamnern Stadium (Muay Thai)
items.description: The world's first purpose-built Muay Thai stadium, where an evening card opens with the ritual wai kru dance to live music. The most storied, authentic place to see Thailand's national sport; ringside seats put you in the thick of it, and it is a genuine spectacle for a first-timer.

items.name: Khon masked dance at Sala Chalermkrung
items.description: The centuries-old royal masked dance-drama, retelling the Ramakien (Thai Ramayana) with ornate costumes and precise gesture, staged in a landmark 1933 theatre. A refined, unmistakably Thai evening of culture; the Ramayana story is familiar and resonant for Indian visitors.

items.name: Calypso Cabaret
items.description: Bangkok's best-known ladyboy cabaret, a glossy hour of song, dance and impersonation of global icons. Light, fun and family-workable as an evening's entertainment, easily combined with dinner and a stroll at Asiatique.

items.name: Thai cooking class
items.description: The best classes start with a guided market tour to choose lemongrass, galangal and chillies, then walk you through a green curry, tom yum and mango sticky rice you eat together. A hands-on half-day the whole family enjoys; most schools happily run fully vegetarian or Jain-friendly menus if asked ahead.

items.name: Traditional Thai massage at Wat Pho
items.description: Take your massage where the art is taught: the school inside Wat Pho is the recognised home of traditional Thai massage, and an hour here is authentic, superb value and part of the temple visit itself. The gentle starting point before the grander spas.

items.name: Divana Spa
items.description: A garden-villa spa group that has become Bangkok's benchmark for the luxury Thai spa experience, with long signature aromatherapy rituals in private, tranquil rooms. Ideal for a couple's afternoon or an unhurried treat; book a signature package ahead as it is deservedly popular.

items.name: Ayutthaya day trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic City of Ayutthaya
items.description: The ruined former capital of Siam, a plain of brick temple spires and the world-famous Buddha head cradled in fig-tree roots at Wat Mahathat. About 90 minutes by road; a private car and guide (often combined with the Bang Pa-In summer palace) makes for an unhurried, air-conditioned day into the heart of Thai history.

items.name: Kanchanaburi & the River Kwai
items.description: The sobering WWII Death Railway, the Bridge over the River Kwai and the moving war cemeteries and Hellfire Pass memorial, set against a beautiful river valley. Many trips add the seven-tier Erawan Waterfall for a swim; a long but rewarding private day, or better as an overnight to a riverside resort.

items.name: Amphawa Floating Market
items.description: The floating market locals actually use, where wooden shophouses and canal-side stalls come alive on Friday-to-Sunday afternoons with grilled prawns and seafood cooked from the boats. Stay past dusk for the long-tail firefly cruise; more authentic and atmospheric than the tourist floating markets.

items.name: Maeklong Railway Market
items.description: A working fresh market laid out directly on live railway tracks: several times a day vendors calmly fold back their awnings as the train inches through, then reopen behind it. A genuinely astonishing few minutes, usually combined with Amphawa or Damnoen Saduak on the same morning.

items.name: Damnoen Saduak Floating Market
items.description: The postcard floating market of laden paddle boats jamming narrow canals, at its best if you arrive before 9am and hire a quiet private paddle boat rather than a motorised one. Touristy but iconic; treat it as a photogenic early stop paired with the Maeklong railway market nearby.

items.name: Sorn
items.description: The first Thai restaurant in the world to hold three Michelin stars, Southern Thai cooking raised to the summit.

items.name: Gaggan
items.description: Progressive Indian theatre from Gaggan Anand, five times crowned the best restaurant in Asia.

items.name: Sühring
items.description: Twin German brothers reimagining the food of their childhood, in a garden villa.

items.name: Nusara
items.description: Chef Ton's love letter to his grandmother's cooking, with Wat Pho glowing through the window.

items.name: Potong
items.description: Chef Pam's Thai-Chinese story told across five floors of her family's old medicine shophouse.

items.name: Le Du
items.description: The kitchen that launched Bangkok's modern-Thai movement, still setting the pace.

items.name: Chef's Table by Vincent Thierry
items.description: Refined French dining 61 floors up, where the whole city drops away beneath you.

items.name: Mezzaluna
items.description: A sky-high room marrying French and Japanese technique on the 65th floor.

items.name: R-Haan
items.description: Royal-Thai cooking staged with ceremony, the old recipes, kept alive and exact.

items.name: GAA
items.description: Chef Garima Arora's fearless, ingredient-led cooking, the first Indian woman to win a Michelin star.

items.name: Côte by Mauro Colagreco
items.description: The Mirazur master's Riviera seafood, brought to the Chao Phraya's edge.

items.name: Gaggan at Louis Vuitton
items.description: Gaggan Anand inside the maison itself, dinner as a one-off collaboration between chef and house.

items.name: Le Normandie by Alain Roux
items.description: Grand riverside French dining in the Oriental's most storied room.

items.name: Sushi Masato
items.description: Bangkok's most sought-after sushi counter, Tokyo-grade omakase, near-impossible to book.

items.name: Maison Dunand
items.description: Swiss-French haute cuisine in a converted mansion, plated with quiet rigour.

items.name: Blue by Alain Ducasse
items.description: The Ducasse standard on the river, classical French precision with a Bangkok view.

items.name: Baan Tepa
items.description: A home turned restaurant, cooking Thai food with a farm's rhythm and a family's warmth.

items.name: Samrub Samrub Thai
items.description: A research kitchen recovering lost Thai recipes, one seasonal menu at a time.

items.name: Nahm
items.description: One of the world's defining modern-Thai kitchens, exacting and unafraid of real heat.

items.name: Paste Bangkok
items.description: Antique Thai recipes, painstakingly researched and plated with a jeweller's care.

items.name: Saneh Jaan
items.description: Regional Thai home cooking, gently refined, comfort with a Michelin star.

items.name: Aksorn
items.description: Old Thai cookbooks brought back to the table by chef David Thompson.

items.name: Chim by Siam Wisdom
items.description: A teak-house kitchen guarding the grand old recipes of Thai gastronomy.

items.name: Mia
items.description: A young couple's inventive, ingredient-driven cooking that keeps its star with ease.

items.name: Haoma
items.description: Zero-waste, neo-Indian cooking grown in the restaurant's own urban farm.

items.name: Inddee
items.description: Regional Indian cooking with a modern hand, and a rare Bangkok star for the cuisine.

items.name: Igniv Bangkok
items.description: Andreas Caminada's shared-plate fine dining, generous, playful, refined.

items.name: Elements, Inspired by Ciel Bleu
items.description: French–Japanese cooking with skyline views from the Okura tower.

items.name: Signature
items.description: A refined French-leaning kitchen that quietly holds its star year on year.

items.name: Wana Yook
items.description: Family Thai recipes served in a heritage shophouse, warm and unhurried.

items.name: Nawa
items.description: Refined regional Thai cooking with a riverside sensibility.

items.name: Avant
items.description: A modern, boundary-pushing kitchen newly welcomed into the Michelin fold.

items.name: Coda
items.description: An inventive new one-star doing quiet, considered tasting menus.

items.name: Goat
items.description: A characterful newcomer that charmed the inspectors into a first star.

items.name: Jay Fai
items.description: The goggle-wearing grandmother who cooks her crab omelette over charcoal, and holds a Michelin star for it.
Thai ingredients, modern technique and a young, restless kitchen in old Chinatown.

items.name: Err
items.description: Urban-rustic Thai drinking food and grilled snacks from the Bo.lan team, by the river.

items.name: Prai Raya
items.description: Phuketian Southern-Thai cooking, the famous crab curry and turmeric-rich dishes.

items.name: Baan (by Chef Sujira 'Aom' Pongmorn)
items.description: Comforting family-recipe Thai cooking, the kind grandmothers guard.

items.name: Thipsamai
items.description: Bangkok's most famous pad thai, wrapped in a thin egg skin since 1966.

items.name: Krua Apsorn
items.description: Central-Thai home cooking beloved by locals, the crab-and-yellow-chilli stir-fry is legend.

items.name: Sanguan Sri
items.description: A no-frills lunchroom serving proper old-Bangkok curries to office crowds since the 1960s.

items.name: Polo Fried Chicken (Soi Polo)
items.description: Crisp fried chicken buried under fried garlic, a Bangkok lunch pilgrimage.

items.name: The Bamboo Bar, Mandarin Oriental
items.description: Bangkok's original jazz bar since 1953, in the grande dame of the river, the city's most storied room for a drink.

items.name: Bar Us
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars (No. 4, 2025), Thailand's best bar
items.description: The bar the region rates above all others in Bangkok right now, precise, personal, and quietly brilliant.

items.name: Dry Wave Cocktail Studio
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars (No. 5, 2025), Highest New Entry Award
items.description: The city's most talked-about newcomer, a studio-like counter that vaulted straight into the region's top five.

items.name: BKK Social Club, Four Seasons
items.description: A golden-age Buenos Aires grand café on the river, inside the Four Seasons, glamour done with real substance.

items.name: Vesper
credentials: Rémy Martin Legend of the List Award 2025
items.description: Silom's most serious cocktail room, holding its own since 2014 with an aperitivo sensibility and quiet mastery.

items.name: Opium Bar
items.description: A speakeasy over the top floors of a 120-year-old shophouse that was once an opium den, drinks with a Chinatown soul.

items.name: Bar Sathorn, The House on Sathorn
items.description: Modern mixology inside an 1889 mansion that has been a merchant's home, a hotel and an embassy, history in a glass.

items.name: Mahaniyom Cocktail Club
items.description: A Thai-ingredient-led bar that has ranked among Asia's very best, refined, seasonal, deeply of this place.

items.name: Sky Bar, lebua at State Tower
credentials: World's highest outdoor rooftop bar; setting of 'The Hangover Part II'
items.description: The open-air perch 63 floors up that the world knows from film, the definitive Bangkok skyline drink.

items.name: Vertigo & Moon Bar, Banyan Tree
credentials: Landmark Bangkok rooftop atop the 61-storey Banyan Tree, Sathorn
items.description: An open-edge deck on the 61st floor with nothing between you and the whole of Bangkok.

items.name: Ojo, The Standard
credentials: Rooftop bar-restaurant on the 76th floor of King Power MahaNakhon
items.description: A vivid rooftop 76 floors up in the city's most striking tower, the highest of Bangkok's serious sky bars.

items.name: GOD (Genius.On.Drugs)
items.description: A run-down-cathedral cocktail temple on Chinatown's edgiest lane, creative, theatrical, open late.

plan.heading: 4 days in Bangkok, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle in at The Siam or Capella Bangkok on the river, then take the hotel boat to Wat Pho for the reclining Buddha before the coaches arrive.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross to the Grand Palace and Wat Arun, then a slow longtail through the Thonburi khlongs away from the tourist stretch.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Sühring, the twin brothers' modern German-Thai table in a garden villa, with cocktails after at BKK Social Club.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Early to Or Tor Kor market for fruit and curries, then the Jim Thompson House to understand Thai silk and the man who revived it.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private appointment at a silk atelier or a session with a Bangkok tailor, followed by quiet time at your hotel spa.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Le Du, Chef Ton's Thai tasting menu ranked among Asia's best, then a nightcap at Mahaniyom or Tep Bar for live phin.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Coffee and the galleries around Charoenkrung and the Bangkok CityCity Gallery, the city's serious contemporary art quarter.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Potong, then browse the design shops of Ekkamai and Thonglor at an unhurried pace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Gaggan Anand's newest room, the theatrical benchmark of the city, booked well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A calm morning at Wat Benchamabophit, the marble temple, before the heat, then a final Thai breakfast at the hotel.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A leisurely lunch of boat noodles or a last massage, then unhurried packing.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early supper of street-side pad thai at Thipsamai before the airport transfer.

items.name: Riverside (Charoenkrung)
items.description: The grand river hotels and the old trading quarter; the most atmospheric base and best for temples by boat.

items.name: Sukhumvit
items.description: The modern spine of dining, bars and shopping on the skytrain; convenient and cosmopolitan.

items.name: Old City (Rattanakosin)
items.description: Walking distance to the Grand Palace and Wat Pho; for those who want history on the doorstep over nightlife.

events.name: Songkran
events.note: Thai New Year, marked by temple blessings and city-wide water fights; joyous but book far ahead and expect to get wet.

events.name: Loy Krathong
events.note: The festival of lights, when candlelit floats are set adrift on the river and canals across the city at dusk.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay along the river (Mandarin Oriental, Capella) or in quiet Sathorn rather than the Sukhumvit crush; dress covers shoulders and knees for the Grand Palace and temples, and the wet season runs June to October.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You land at Suvarnabhumi (BKK); a chauffeured car meets you airside and clears you to a private limousine in twenty minutes, or a helicopter transfer covers the city in under fifteen.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Keep a private car and driver on call for the sprawl, and use the BTS Skytrain or a river boat only when traffic makes the Chao Phraya the faster line.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Buy an AIS or TrueMove eSIM before you fly; 5G is strong citywide and hotel wifi is reliable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Thai baht (THB); cards are taken everywhere upscale but keep cash for markets and drivers, and a small rounded tip is appreciated though never expected.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to February is the cool, dry window and the only time the heat relents; skip April to October, when the monsoon and pre-monsoon humidity make the city heavy and wet.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi and Mumbai in about 4h 25m. Thai Airways and Air India fly it in a proper business cabin; Thai's Royal Silk product and its Bangkok home lounges are the smoother choice. If you connect onward in Asia, BKK is an easy hub with good premium lounges.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; keep routine jabs current and consider Hepatitis A and Typhoid. Safe and easy for private travellers. Drink bottled or filtered water only; tap is not for drinking.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Very easy for vegetarians and workable for Jain with clear instruction, though fish sauce is near-universal, so specify. Excellent Indian food across the city. Saras and Rang Mahal (Rembrandt) are dependable for refined Indian; Broccoli Revolution is a strong all-vegetarian option.
